screens.title: Two needles, every sentence
lines: A sentence is knitting: the SUBJECT and the PREDICATE are your two needles — who or what it's about, and what it does.
Drop a needle and the row unravels into a fragment; jam two rows together without a legal join and you've knitted a run-on.

vocab.meaning: who or what the sentence is about
what the subject does or is
an incomplete sentence — a dropped stitch missing its subject or predicate
two complete sentences jammed together without a legal join

sequences.title: Word Roots: Crack One, Unlock Dozens

screens.title: Word-parts carry meaning
lines: In Duolingo Swahili, mtoto is one child and watoto is many — the word-part does the talking.
English plays the same game with Greek and Latin ROOTS: crack one root and you unlock dozens of words at once.

vocab.meaning: the meaning-carrying core of a word, like bene (good) or aud (hear)
a word-part attached before the root, like mal- or tele-
hints in the surrounding sentence that reveal what an unknown word means

screens.title: The essay cathedral
lines: A five-paragraph essay is a cathedral: the hook is the doorway, the body paragraphs are pillars, the conclusion rings the bell — and the THESIS is the spine holding it all up.
Pingry hands you this blueprint in sixth grade; today you learn to read it like an architect.

vocab.meaning: the one arguable sentence your whole essay defends
the opening sentence of a body paragraph, announcing its one job
an opening line that pulls the reader through the doorway
a signpost word showing how ideas connect — however, therefore, for example

items.prompt: Let's knit a sentence together — and watch what happens when a needle drops.

steps.text: Knit with me: 'The kitten pounced on the yarn.' Needle one, the SUBJECT: 'The kitten' — who it's about. Needle two, the PREDICATE: 'pounced on the yarn' — what it did.
Drop the subject needle and the row unravels: 'Pounced on the yarn.' Who pounced?! That's a FRAGMENT — it cannot stand alone.

check.question: Why is 'Pounced on the yarn' a fragment?
options: It has no subject — nobody is doing the pouncing
It is too short to be a sentence
It needs an adjective

steps.text: Opposite problem: two complete rows jammed together. 'The kitten pounced the yarn unraveled' is a RUN-ON; with only a comma between them ('The kitten pounced, the yarn unraveled'), it's called a comma SPLICE.
Three legal joins: a period. A semicolon. Or a comma + joining word (and, but, so).

check.question: Which version is legally joined?
options: The kitten pounced, and the yarn unraveled.
The kitten pounced, the yarn unraveled.
The kitten pounced and, the yarn unraveled.

items.prompt: Your turn on the needles: label the two halves of 'My oldest cat sleeps in the yarn basket.'

lines: Subject (who or what it's about): My oldest [[cat]]
Predicate (what the subject does): [[sleeps]] in the yarn basket

items.hint: Ask WHO first; then ask what that who is up to.
items.explanation: Subject = 'my oldest cat,' predicate = 'sleeps in the yarn basket' — both needles present, so the row holds.

items.prompt: Repair shop: fix the jammed rows in 'The timer beeped, the cookies were done.'

lines: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences — that error is called a comma [[splice]].
Legal fix: 'The timer beeped, [[and|so]] the cookies were done.'

items.hint: Name the error first (you just met it), then give the comma a joining-word partner.
items.explanation: A comma needs a partner like 'and' or 'so' to join complete sentences — alone, it's a splice.

items.prompt: Find the SUBJECT: 'The fluffy gray cat napped on the warm laundry.'
options: The fluffy gray cat
napped on the warm laundry
the warm laundry
napped
items.hint: Ask: who or what is this sentence about?
items.explanation: The subject is who or what the sentence is about — here, that magnificent cat. 'Napped on the warm laundry' is the predicate.

items.prompt: Which of these is a COMPLETE sentence?
items.answer: The yarn rolled under the couch.
options: The yarn rolled under the couch.
Rolling under the couch.
Because the yarn rolled.
Under the couch, near the dust.
items.hint: Check both needles: a subject AND a predicate.
items.explanation: 'The yarn rolled under the couch' has a subject (the yarn) and a predicate (rolled…) — the others are fragments missing a needle.

items.prompt: Sort each word into its part of speech.
items.hint: Nouns name, verbs do, adjectives describe.
items.explanation: Nouns name people, places, and things; verbs show action; adjectives describe nouns.

items.prompt: Type the correct word: their, there, or they're.

lines: The cats groomed [[their]] whiskers after dinner.

items.hint: You need the word that shows the whiskers BELONG to the cats.
items.explanation: 'Their' shows ownership; 'there' points to a place, and 'they're' is short for 'they are.'

items.prompt: Find the PREDICATE: 'Every owl in the tower hooted at midnight.'
options: hooted at midnight
Every owl in the tower
in the tower
Every owl
items.hint: The predicate tells what the subject DID.
items.explanation: 'Hooted at midnight' is what the owls did — that's the predicate; 'every owl in the tower' is the whole subject.

items.prompt: Sort these words from a fan's concert diary into parts of speech.
items.hint: Adverbs often end in -ly and tell HOW something happens.
items.explanation: Adverbs describe how, when, or where an action happens — 'gently' and 'loudly' modify verbs, while adjectives stick to nouns.

items.prompt: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause — a thought that leans on a main clause?
options: Because the oven timer beeped
The oven timer beeped
The cookies are ready
We grabbed the oven mitts
items.hint: Read each one aloud — which leaves you waiting to hear what happened?
items.explanation: 'Because' turns a complete thought into a leaner: 'Because the oven timer beeped…' — then WHAT?! It needs a main clause to hold it up.

items.prompt: One segment hides an apostrophe error. Tap it.
items.hint: Expand the apostrophe: does 'it is' make sense there?
items.explanation: 'It's' always means 'it is' — here you want the possessive 'its': the tarts belong to the bakery.

items.prompt: Fill in each blank: your or you're?

lines: [[You're]] going to love this chapter — bring [[your]] bookmark.

items.hint: One of them is secretly 'you are' wearing a trench coat.
items.explanation: 'You're' = 'you are'; 'your' shows the bookmark belongs to you.

items.prompt: Fix this run-on: 'The encore ended, the fans kept chanting.'
items.answer: The encore ended, but the fans kept chanting.
options: The encore ended, but the fans kept chanting.
The encore ended, the fans, kept chanting.
The encore ended the fans kept chanting.
The encore, ended, but the fans kept chanting.
items.hint: A comma alone can't weld two sentences — it needs a conjunction partner.
items.explanation: Comma + 'but' legally joins the two complete thoughts. Removing the comma just fuses them, and the extra commas chop the sentence in the wrong places.

items.prompt: Amal wrote: 'I baked treats for my parents, two cats and a wizard.' How should she punctuate it so her parents are NOT the two cats and the wizard?
items.answer: I baked treats for my parents, two cats, and a wizard.
options: I baked treats for my parents, two cats, and a wizard.
I baked treats for my parents two cats and a wizard.
I baked treats, for my parents, two cats and a wizard.
I baked treats for my parents, two cats and, a wizard.
items.hint: A comma before the final 'and' separates the last two list members.
items.explanation: That last comma (the serial comma) makes a clear list of three: parents, cats, wizard. Without it, the sentence can read as if her parents ARE two cats and a wizard!

items.prompt: Match each comma rule to the sentence that shows it.

pairs: We packed yarn, needles, and snacks.
After the rain stopped, we walked to the library.
My cat, a true menace, stole the wool.
I knitted a row, and Dad iced the cake.

items.hint: Look at WHERE the commas sit in each sentence.
items.explanation: Lists, introductions, interrupters, and compound sentences — four different jobs for one tiny mark.

items.prompt: Word-Pick Lightning! Type the word that fits each sentence.
items.hint: Expand contractions in your head: they're = they are, it's = it is.
items.explanation: Fast checks win: expand the contraction, then ask if you mean ownership, place, time, or comparison.

items.prompt: Exactly one segment has a confused word. Tap it.
items.hint: Try swapping in 'they are' and listen to the sentence.
items.explanation: 'Delivered they are letters' makes no sense — it should be the possessive 'their,' because the letters belong to someone.

items.prompt: In 'Although the yarn was hopelessly tangled, Amal finished the sleeve before bedtime,' which part is the DEPENDENT clause?
items.answer: Although the yarn was hopelessly tangled
options: Although the yarn was hopelessly tangled
Amal finished the sleeve
Amal finished the sleeve before bedtime
before bedtime
items.hint: Which chunk has a subject and a verb but still can't stand alone?
items.explanation: 'Although' makes that clause lean on the main one — it has a subject and verb but leaves you hanging by itself. 'Before bedtime' is only a phrase, with no subject-verb pair.

items.prompt: Choose the BEST repair: 'Amal practiced the choreography for two hours her legs felt like noodles.'
items.answer: Amal practiced the choreography for two hours; her legs felt like noodles.
options: Amal practiced the choreography for two hours; her legs felt like noodles.
Amal practiced the choreography for two hours, her legs felt like noodles.
Amal practiced the choreography, for two hours her legs felt like noodles.
Amal practiced the choreography for two hours her legs, felt like noodles.
items.hint: Two complete thoughts need a real boundary: period, semicolon, or comma + joining word.
items.explanation: A semicolon is a legal weld between two related complete thoughts. A comma alone just trades the fused sentence for a comma splice.

items.prompt: Fill in each blank: affect or effect?

lines: The storm didn't [[affect]] our plans, and candlelight gave the reading nook a magical [[effect]].

items.hint: Affect is the Action (a verb); effect is the End result (a noun).
items.explanation: 'Affect' acts — it's the verb meaning 'to influence.' 'Effect' is the noun result, the thing you end up with.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about clauses — tap the LIE.

truths: An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.
Words like 'because' and 'although' turn a clause into a dependent one.
data.lie: If a group of words is long enough, it counts as a complete sentence.

items.hint: Can a sentence's completeness be measured in inches?
items.explanation: Length is a decoy — 'Run!' is a complete sentence, while 'the enormous dragon sleeping on the mountain of gold' is still a fragment. Completeness needs a subject plus a predicate, not a word count.

items.prompt: Fill in each blank: its or it's?

lines: The dragon stretched [[its]] wings — [[it's]] grumpy when travelers wake it.

items.hint: If 'it is' fits, use the apostrophe; ownership gets none.
items.explanation: 'Its' (no apostrophe) is possessive, like 'his.' 'It's' is only ever the contraction of 'it is.'

items.prompt: Repair this run-on like an editor: 'The yarn rolled away, the kitten gave chase.'

lines: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma — that's a comma [[splice]].
Fix one: 'The yarn rolled away, [[so|and]] the kitten gave chase.'
Fix two: swap the comma for a [[semicolon|;]].

items.hint: Name the crime first, then pick a legal weld.
items.explanation: A comma needs a conjunction partner (so/and), or you can upgrade to a semicolon — either turns the splice into a legal sentence.

items.prompt: Legendary: which sentence means MORE THAN ONE cat shares the yarn basket?
items.answer: The cats' yarn basket tipped over.
options: The cats' yarn basket tipped over.
The cat's yarn basket tipped over.
The cats's yarn basket tipped over.
The cat yarn's basket tipped over.
items.hint: Where the apostrophe sits tells you how many owners there are.
items.explanation: Apostrophe AFTER the s = plural owners (cats'); before the s = one cat. Position is everything.

items.prompt: Legendary triple: complete the fan-club update with then, than, or lose.

lines: If the tour tickets cost more [[than]] we saved, [[then]] we'll stream the concert from home — either way, we won't [[lose]] our spot in the fan club.

items.hint: 'Than' compares; 'then' tells when; 'lose' is the opposite of win (one o!).
items.explanation: Comparison takes 'than,' sequence takes 'then,' and 'lose' (one o) means to misplace or be defeated — 'loose' means not tight.

items.prompt: Legendary: which sentence is punctuated perfectly?
items.answer: My broom, an ancient Comet 140, still beats its rivals in a dive.
options: My broom, an ancient Comet 140, still beats its rivals in a dive.
My broom an ancient Comet 140, still beats its rivals in a dive.
My broom, an ancient Comet 140 still beats it's rivals in a dive.
My broom, an ancient Comet 140, still beats it's rivals in a dive.
items.hint: Check two things: the PAIR of commas around the interrupter, and the apostrophe.
items.explanation: The interrupter 'an ancient Comet 140' needs commas on BOTH sides, and possessive 'its' takes no apostrophe.

items.prompt: Legendary: combine into ONE correct sentence using a dependent clause: 'The kitten was curious. The kitten opened the cabinet. The flour spilled.'
items.answer: Because the curious kitten opened the cabinet, the flour spilled.
options: Because the curious kitten opened the cabinet, the flour spilled.
The curious kitten opened the cabinet, the flour spilled.
The kitten was curious she opened the cabinet and the flour spilled.
Because the curious kitten opened the cabinet. The flour spilled.
items.hint: The winner starts with 'Because…' AND stays attached to a main clause.
items.explanation: 'Because…cabinet' is a dependent clause correctly attached to its main clause with a comma. The rivals are a comma splice, a fused run-on, and a stranded fragment.

items.prompt: Legendary edit: exactly one segment creates a comma splice. Tap it.

segments: My cat adores the knitting basket,

items.hint: 'And refuses' is innocent — a verb may share its subject. Where does a brand-new sentence sneak in after a mere comma?
items.explanation: 'She burrows…' starts a second complete sentence after only a comma — that's the splice. Fix: a semicolon, or 'basket, where she burrows.'

items.prompt: Word-cracking, Duolingo-style: what does 'benevolent' mean in 'The benevolent witch left warm bread out for tired travelers'?

steps.text: In Swahili, mtoto is one child and watoto is many — the word-part carries the meaning. English hides meaning in word-parts too: Greek and Latin ROOTS.
Spot the root: bene- is Latin for 'good' or 'well.' You already know it from benefit (a good thing) and benefactor (a do-gooder).

check.question: What does the root bene- tell you about 'benevolent'?
options: Something about goodness is baked into the word
The word has to do with bread
The word is about size

steps.text: Now add context clues: she 'left warm bread out for tired travelers.' Root says GOOD + context shows kindness → benevolent means kind and generous.
That's the two-key unlock: ROOT + CONTEXT. Crack one root and you can pick the lock on its whole word family.

check.question: Swap bene- for mal- ('bad'): a MALevolent witch is one who…
options: wishes harm on others
bakes badly
travels a lot

items.prompt: Your turn: crack 'audible' in 'The kitten's purr was barely audible across the room.'

lines: Root: aud = hear (audio, audience, auditorium)
Suffix: -ible = able to be
So the purr could barely be [[heard]].

items.hint: aud shows up in AUDio — what do you do with audio?
items.explanation: aud (hear) + -ible (able to be) = able to be heard. Root families always share their core meaning.

items.prompt: Crack two roots at once: port (porter, transport) and dict (dictate, dictionary).

lines: A hotel porter [[carries]] your bags — port = carry.
To dictate a letter is to [[say]] it aloud while someone writes — dict = say.

items.hint: What does a porter DO with luggage? What does your mouth do when you dictate?
items.explanation: port = carry and dict = say — now transport, import, predict, and contradict all crack open.

items.prompt: Benefit, benevolent, benefactor — the Latin root bene- means…
options: good or well
money
friendly animals
two
items.hint: A BENEfit is a ___ thing that helps you.
items.explanation: bene = good/well, so the whole family glows: benefit (a good thing), benevolent (kind), benefactor (a do-gooder).

items.prompt: Match each root to its meaning.
items.hint: Think of one familiar word for each: transport, predict, audio, visible.
items.explanation: Roots are reusable bricks: transport, dictate, audible, and visible all snap together from these four.

items.prompt: Use the context clue: 'Kittens were abundant at the shelter this spring — every cage, basket, and lap seemed to hold three.' Abundant means…
options: present in large amounts
very rare
sleepy
noisy
items.hint: The second half of the sentence paints the picture — lots, or few?
items.explanation: The clue 'every cage, basket, and lap' shows overflow — abundant means plentiful.

items.prompt: Build the word: port (carry) + -able (able to be).

lines: A speaker you can carry to dance practice is [[portable]].

items.hint: Just snap the two word-parts together.
items.explanation: port + able = portable, 'able to be carried' — roots are word-building bricks.

items.prompt: Sort the words by their root: vis/vid (see) or aud (hear).
items.hint: Say each word — does it belong to eyes or ears?
items.explanation: vis/vid words are eye-words; aud words are ear-words. An audience was originally a group of listeners!

items.prompt: Halfway through a lesson, the app flashed 'MALFUNCTION' and froze. The root mal- tells you the app is…
options: working badly
working fast
finished updating
brand new
items.hint: Mal- is the evil twin of bene-.
items.explanation: mal = bad, so malfunction = working badly. The same root lurks in malevolent and malodorous (bad-smelling).

items.prompt: Match each Greek root to its meaning.
items.hint: Telephone = sound from far away. That's two of them cracked already.
items.explanation: Greek roots power the science shelf: chronology, hydrate, geology, telescope, phonics.

items.prompt: Context clue: 'Though she usually loved starting new patterns, Amal was reluctant to unravel three days of careful knitting.' Reluctant means…
options: unwilling and hesitant
excited and eager
skilled and quick
careless and rushed
items.hint: The word 'though' signals a contrast with 'usually loved.'
items.explanation: 'Though' flips the direction: she usually loves starting, but here she hesitates — reluctant means unwilling.

items.prompt: Sort by root: scrib/script (write) or dict (say).
items.hint: Is the action done with a pen or with a voice?
items.explanation: scrib/script words live on paper; dict words come out of mouths. A prediction is something 'said before' it happens.

items.prompt: Spectator, inspect, spectacles — the root spect means…
options: to look or watch
to walk
to build
to cheer
items.hint: What does a spectator DO at a quidditch match?
items.explanation: spect = look/watch: a spectator watches, you inspect by looking closely, and spectacles help you see.

items.prompt: Type the power word: the opposite of abundant, meaning 'in short supply.'

lines: By August, the shop's softest wool was [[scarce]] — only two skeins left on the shelf.

items.hint: Six letters, starts with 's' — the clue is 'only two skeins left.'
items.explanation: Scarce means hard to find, in short supply — the empty shelf is the giveaway clue.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about word roots — tap the LIE.

truths: 'Telephone' is built from roots meaning 'far away' + 'sound.'
'Geography' contains geo, the Greek root for earth.
data.lie: 'Audience' comes from a root meaning 'to see.'

items.hint: Which sense does an audience originally use?
items.explanation: Audience comes from aud, 'to hear' — literally a group of listeners. The seeing root is vis/vid, as in 'video.'

items.prompt: Root Lightning! Type the meaning of each root.
items.hint: One familiar word per root: benefit, audio, video, transport…
items.explanation: Twelve roots, hundreds of words unlocked — that's an excellent exchange rate.

items.prompt: Context: 'The label promised the potion would grant perfect recall, but Priya was skeptical — no brew had ever helped her remember where she left her wand.' Skeptical means…
options: doubtful that something is true
completely convinced
terrified
forgetful
items.hint: The word 'but' plus her past experience tells you how much she believes the label.
items.explanation: Her experience contradicts the promise, so she doubts it — skeptical means questioning whether something is really true.

items.prompt: Using the root chron (time), what is a 'chronicle'?
items.answer: a record of events in the order they happened
options: a record of events in the order they happened
a clock that runs backward
a list sorted alphabetically
a brand-new invention
items.hint: chron = time; a chronicle organizes events by it.
items.explanation: A chronicle records events in time order — same root family as chronological and synchronize.

items.prompt: Crack the science words: type each root's meaning.

lines: Biology studies living things because bio means [[life]].
Geology digs into rocks because geo means [[earth]].

items.hint: A BIOgraphy is the story of someone's ___.
items.explanation: bio = life and geo = earth — every '-ology' is just 'the study of' plus a root.

items.prompt: Context: 'The cardamom in the cake was so subtle that only Grandma, with her baker's tongue, noticed it under the vanilla.' Subtle means…
options: faint and not obvious
overpowering
bitter
missing entirely
items.hint: Only ONE expert taster caught it — was the flavor loud or quiet?
items.explanation: If only the sharpest taster detects it, the flavor is delicate and easy to miss — that's subtle.

items.prompt: Sort by root: micro (small), mega (huge), or tele (far).
items.hint: A megastar's voice through a megaphone is anything but small.
items.explanation: micro shrinks, mega supersizes, tele stretches across distance — a telescope is literally a 'far-seer.'

items.prompt: Context: 'The dream was so vivid that at breakfast she could still smell the dragon smoke and count the castle's torches.' Vivid means…
options: intensely clear and lifelike
quickly forgotten
in black and white
frightening
items.hint: She remembers smells AND exact details — how sharp is that dream?
items.explanation: Smelling smoke and counting torches after waking means the dream felt real — vivid means strikingly clear and lifelike, not necessarily scary.

items.prompt: Crack a wizard word: 'The scroll bore a malediction — whoever opened it would itch for a week.'

lines: Break it apart: mal = [[bad]] and dict = [[say]].
So a malediction is words spoken to wish harm — a curse.

items.hint: You already own both bricks: malfunction and dictate.
items.explanation: mal (bad) + dict (say) = 'bad-saying,' a curse. Its opposite, benediction, is a blessing.

items.prompt: Legendary: the museum card reads, 'The champions' cup was inscribed with the names of every winner since 1894.' Using scrib/script, 'inscribed' means…
items.answer: had words written or carved onto it
options: had words written or carved onto it
was polished until it shone
was hidden away for safekeeping
was sold at auction
items.hint: scrib/script always involves writing — where is the writing here?
items.explanation: in (onto) + scrib (write): the winners' names were written onto the cup. Manuscript and inscription share the same brick.

items.prompt: Legendary: 'With three curious cats and one dangling ball of mohair left on the table, the great yarn tangle was inevitable.' Inevitable means…
items.answer: certain to happen, impossible to avoid
options: certain to happen, impossible to avoid
easy to clean up
extremely surprising
somebody's fault
items.hint: Three cats + dangling yarn — what are the odds of escape?
items.explanation: The setup allows only one outcome — inevitable means unavoidable, certain to happen.

items.prompt: Legendary match: pair each power word with its meaning.
items.hint: Lock in the pairs you're sure of first — strategy beats luck.
items.explanation: These five show up all over grade-6 reading — collect them like rare cards.

items.prompt: Legendary invention: a wizard catalog sells a 'chronophone.' Using its roots, what would this gadget do?
items.answer: let you hear sounds from another time
options: let you hear sounds from another time
measure how much water you drink
project giant images of the earth
write letters automatically
items.hint: chron + phon — you've already unlocked both bricks.
items.explanation: chron (time) + phon (sound) = a time-sound machine. Root-stacking decodes even words that don't exist yet — that's real word power.

items.prompt: Legendary: 'Her brother's streak died in a week, but Amal was diligent: 412 days of Swahili, every lesson reviewed twice, even on her birthday.' Diligent means…
options: showing steady, careful effort
naturally talented
competitive with family
obsessed with birthdays
items.hint: The colon introduces the evidence — what do 412 days and double reviews prove?
items.explanation: The evidence shows steady, careful, day-after-day work — diligence is about effort, not talent.

items.prompt: Let's judge thesis statements like architects — which spine can hold up a whole essay?

steps.text: A thesis must be ARGUABLE (someone could disagree) and SPECIFIC (it names its reasons). 'Cats are animals' fails instantly — nobody can argue with a fact.

Candidate: 'Cats are the ideal pet for book lovers because they are quiet, independent, and happy to sit still for whole chapters.' Arguable? Yes — a dog person would object. Specific? Yes — three named reasons.

check.question: Why does 'Cats are animals' fail as a thesis?
options: It's a fact nobody can argue against
It's too short to be a sentence
It shouldn't mention animals

steps.text: Each reason becomes a pillar: body paragraph 1 = quiet, 2 = independent, 3 = chapter-length lap naps. The spine decides the whole skeleton.
So the test is two questions: could someone disagree? And do I know exactly what each body paragraph will prove?

check.question: 'Some people have pets' — what's the main problem with this thesis?
options: It isn't arguable or specific, so it can't organize an essay
It's about people instead of animals
It uses the word 'some'

items.prompt: Label the cathedral: complete the essay blueprint.

lines: The doorway that pulls readers in: the [[hook]]
The spine that states your arguable claim: the [[thesis]]
Each pillar (body paragraph) opens with a topic sentence proving one reason.

items.hint: Both answers were just pre-taught — the doorway and the spine.
items.explanation: Hook invites, thesis holds the building up, and topic sentences run the pillars — that's the whole blueprint.

items.prompt: Wire the signposts: connect claim to evidence to conclusion in this mini-paragraph.

lines: Claim: Baking is secretly math homework.
Introduce evidence: '[[For example|For instance]], doubling a recipe means multiplying every fraction in it.'
Show the result: '[[Therefore|So|Thus]], every batch of cookies is a worksheet you can eat.'

items.hint: The first signpost introduces an example; the second announces a conclusion.
items.explanation: 'For example' introduces evidence and 'therefore' signals a result — transitions tell readers which way the road bends.

items.prompt: Stack the cathedral: put the parts of a five-paragraph essay in order.

sequence: Hook — an opening line that grabs the reader
Thesis — the arguable claim the essay will defend
Body paragraph 1 — first reason, with evidence
Body paragraphs 2 and 3 — remaining reasons, with evidence
Conclusion — restate the thesis and close the doors

items.hint: Doorway first, spine right behind it, then pillars, then the bell.
items.explanation: Hook → thesis → body pillars → conclusion: the blueprint never changes, even when the topic does.

items.prompt: Pick the STRONGER thesis for an essay about cats.
items.answer: Cats make better apartment pets than dogs because they are quiet, tidy, and content alone.
options: Cats make better apartment pets than dogs because they are quiet, tidy, and content alone.
Cats are a kind of animal.
I like cats a lot.
This essay will be about cats.
items.hint: Strong = someone could disagree AND it names its reasons.
items.explanation: It's arguable (dog fans, assemble!) and specific — three reasons means three ready-made body paragraphs. The others are a fact, a feeling, and an announcement.

items.prompt: Choose the best transition: 'First, she preheated the oven. ____, she measured the flour and sugar.'
options: Next
However
Therefore
Meanwhile
items.hint: The two steps simply happen in order — no contrast, no cause-and-effect.
items.explanation: It's a sequence of steps, so 'Next' fits; 'however' would promise a contrast and 'therefore' a result.

items.prompt: Sort the phrases: formal essay voice vs. group-chat voice.
items.hint: Which ones could open a sentence for your English teacher?
items.explanation: Formal writing keeps full words and measured claims; chat voice saves its sparkle for friends. Both are real skills — the trick is matching voice to audience.

items.prompt: Which opening line is the strongest HOOK for an essay about libraries?
items.answer: At midnight, the library's book-return slot swallowed my homework — and that's how the best week of my life began.
options: At midnight, the library's book-return slot swallowed my homework — and that's how the best week of my life began.
This essay is about libraries.
Libraries are buildings that hold books.
I will now tell you three facts about libraries.
items.hint: A hook makes you NEED the next sentence.
items.explanation: A midnight mystery demands a next sentence; the others are announcements or flat facts. Curiosity is the doorway.

items.prompt: Which thesis could power a whole five-paragraph essay?
items.answer: K-pop groups succeed worldwide because of disciplined training, multilingual fan outreach, and cinematic music videos.
options: K-pop groups succeed worldwide because of disciplined training, multilingual fan outreach, and cinematic music videos.
K-pop is music from South Korea.
Lots of people stream music nowadays.
BTS debuted in 2013.
items.hint: Two of these are pure facts and one is fog — find the arguable blueprint.
items.explanation: It takes a debatable position and pre-names its three pillars. Facts like a debut year make good EVIDENCE, but they can't be the spine.

items.prompt: A body paragraph will give evidence that cats meow, chirp, and slow-blink to communicate. Which TOPIC SENTENCE should open it?
items.answer: Cats use a surprising range of signals to talk to their humans.
options: Cats use a surprising range of signals to talk to their humans.
Cats are mammals with excellent balance.
My cat is named Mochi.
In conclusion, cats are great.
items.hint: The topic sentence must cover ALL the evidence coming after it.
items.explanation: Meows, chirps, and slow-blinks are all communication signals — the topic sentence announces exactly that one job. The others change the subject or close the essay early.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Baking teaches real math skills.' Which evidence SUPPORTS it best?
items.answer: Halving a recipe means dividing fractions like 3/4 cup by 2.
options: Halving a recipe means dividing fractions like 3/4 cup by 2.
Fresh cookies smell wonderful.
Some famous bakers have TV shows.
Ovens can reach 230 degrees Celsius.
items.hint: Which option shows math actually happening in the kitchen?
items.explanation: Dividing 3/4 by 2 IS math in action — the others are pleasant facts that never touch the claim.

items.prompt: Type the transition that signals CONTRAST.

lines: Knitting looks slow and old-fashioned. [[However|Yet|Nevertheless]], a practiced knitter can finish a sock in a single movie night.

items.hint: You need a U-turn signal, not a green light.
items.explanation: The second sentence pushes against the first, so a contrast signpost like 'however' marks the turn.

items.prompt: Your draft says: 'Hermione revised her essay twice, Ron wrote his during breakfast.' What's the BEST repair?
items.answer: Hermione revised her essay twice, but Ron wrote his during breakfast.
options: Hermione revised her essay twice, but Ron wrote his during breakfast.
Hermione revised her essay twice Ron wrote his during breakfast.
Hermione revised, her essay twice, Ron wrote his during breakfast.
Hermione revised her essay twice but, Ron wrote his during breakfast.
items.hint: Two complete thoughts that clash = comma + a contrast conjunction.
items.explanation: Comma + 'but' both joins the clauses AND highlights the contrast in their study habits. The original comma alone was a splice.

items.prompt: Two truths and a lie about thesis statements — tap the LIE.

truths: A strong thesis takes a position someone could disagree with.
A thesis usually previews the reasons the body paragraphs will prove.
data.lie: A thesis should state a fact that everyone already accepts.

items.hint: Could you write five paragraphs defending 'water is wet'?
items.explanation: If everyone already agrees, there is nothing to defend and the essay has no job. Arguable claims are what give essays a purpose.

items.prompt: Match each transition to the job it does.

pairs: shows two things happening at once

items.hint: Imagine each word as a road sign — what does it warn is coming?
items.explanation: Transitions are signposts: contrast, result, evidence, simultaneous action. Readers steer by them.

items.prompt: Which hook is strongest for an essay arguing that sixth graders should get free reading time?
items.answer: The week our class got twenty minutes of free reading, the room went so silent you could hear pages turn.
options: The week our class got twenty minutes of free reading, the room went so silent you could hear pages turn.
Reading is when you look at words and understand them.
In this essay I will discuss free reading time.
Books have existed for many centuries.
items.hint: Which one drops you inside a scene?
items.explanation: The image of a silent, page-turning classroom pulls the reader in AND quietly previews the argument. Announcements and dictionary facts leave the doorway empty.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Rereading favorite books is valuable, not lazy.' Which evidence supports it BEST?
items.answer: On a second read, you catch foreshadowing and clues you missed the first time.
options: On a second read, you catch foreshadowing and clues you missed the first time.
Some books have beautiful covers.
Many people buy books they never finish.
Libraries let you borrow the same book twice.
items.hint: Find the option that shows a real BENEFIT of the second read.
items.explanation: Catching foreshadowing shows that rereading adds understanding — exactly what 'valuable' claims. The others orbit books without ever proving value.

items.prompt: Trim the fat: 'In my personal opinion, I believe that the bake sale was a successful success.' Which revision fixes the redundancy?
items.answer: I believe the bake sale was a success.
options: I believe the bake sale was a success.
In my personal opinion, I believe that the bake sale was a truly successful success.
The bake sale, in my opinion, I believe, succeeded successfully.
In my opinion I believe the bake sale was successful and a success.
items.hint: Each idea should appear exactly once.
items.explanation: 'In my personal opinion' and 'I believe' say the same thing, and 'successful success' doubles again. One clean claim beats three echoes.

items.prompt: This formal paragraph has one sentence in the wrong VOICE. Tap it.

segments: Shelter cats deserve adoption for three reasons.
First, most arrive already litter trained.
Second, each adoption frees a cage for another rescue.
Also they're like literally the cutest, no cap.

items.hint: Which sentence belongs in a group chat?
items.explanation: Slang like 'no cap' breaks the formal register — try 'Finally, their charm wins over even reluctant visitors.'

items.prompt: Build the body paragraph in order: claim → evidence → explanation → closer.

sequence: Baking strengthens patience like few hobbies can.
For example, real sourdough cannot be rushed — the starter alone takes a week of daily feeding.
That week of waiting trains a baker to trust slow progress instead of quitting.
Patience, it turns out, is the secret ingredient.

items.hint: Topic sentence first; the example needs a claim to support.
items.explanation: Claim, then evidence, then the WHY that ties evidence back to the claim, then a closing beat — pillars are built top-down.

items.prompt: Pick the right signpost: 'The owl reminds me to practice my Swahili every single day. ____, my streak just hit 400.'
options: As a result
On the other hand
For instance
Meanwhile
items.hint: Daily reminders CAUSED the streak — which sign marks cause and effect?
items.explanation: The streak is the RESULT of daily practice, so 'as a result' (a cousin of 'therefore') is the honest signpost. 'On the other hand' would promise a contrast that never comes.

items.prompt: Finish editing this draft so the logic clicks.

lines: Draft: 'I love fantasy novels. Mysteries are my favorite genre.' — these two clash, so join them with a contrast signpost:
'I love fantasy novels; [[however|yet]], mysteries are my favorite genre.'
A result signpost like 'therefore' would be [[wrong|incorrect]] here, because the second sentence pushes against the first.

items.hint: The two sentences disagree — choose the U-turn sign, then say why the green light fails.
items.explanation: 'However' honestly marks the contrast; 'therefore' would promise a cause-and-effect that is not there.

items.prompt: Legendary: four students drafted theses for 'Should wizard schools teach regular math?' Which is STRONGEST?
items.answer: Wizard schools should require math because potion ratios, spell geometry, and quidditch statistics all depend on it.
options: Wizard schools should require math because potion ratios, spell geometry, and quidditch statistics all depend on it.
Math is taught in many schools around the world.
Wizard schools are interesting places with many subjects.
Wizard schools should probably think about possibly adding some subjects.
items.hint: Test each one: arguable? Specific? Could it organize three body paragraphs?
items.explanation: It stakes an arguable claim and pre-names three pillars (ratios, geometry, statistics). The rivals are a fact, a fog bank, and a hedge that never commits.

items.prompt: Legendary: claim — 'Adopting a cat lowers stress.' Three options merely ORBIT the claim; only one SUPPORTS it. Which?
items.answer: A 2019 study found that ten minutes of cat-petting measurably lowered students' cortisol, a stress hormone.
options: A 2019 study found that ten minutes of cat-petting measurably lowered students' cortisol, a stress hormone.
Cats have lived alongside humans for thousands of years.
My neighbor's cat is unusually fluffy and calm.
Cat adoption fees are often cheaper than dog adoption fees.
items.hint: Find the evidence that connects cats to STRESS, not just to cats.
items.explanation: Only the cortisol study links cats to stress reduction with measurable proof. History, one fluffy neighbor-cat, and bargain fees never touch the claim.

items.prompt: Legendary edit: 'The fan project was a big huge success, we collected 200 birthday messages for the singer's birthday.' Choose the BEST revision.
items.answer: The fan project was a huge success: we collected 200 birthday messages for the singer.
options: The fan project was a huge success: we collected 200 birthday messages for the singer.
The fan project was a big huge success; we collected 200 birthday messages for the singer's birthday.
The fan project was a success, we collected 200 messages for the singer's birthday celebration of her birthday.
The fan project, was a big success, we collected 200 birthday messages.
items.hint: Hunt TWO bugs at once: a doubled idea and a comma splice.
items.explanation: 'Big huge' and 'birthday messages… for the birthday' were redundant, and the comma splice needed a real joint — the colon fixes the splice while the trims cut the echoes.

items.prompt: Legendary: arrange the full outline for 'School bake sales should fund the library.'

sequence: Hook: Last year's brownie table earned enough to buy forty new novels.
Thesis: Bake sales should fund the library because demand is high, costs are low, and books outlast cupcakes.
Body 1: Demand — the waitlist for popular series stretches past thirty names.
Body 2: Costs — donated ingredients mean almost every dollar is profit.
Body 3: Lasting value — a twelve-dollar book circulates for years after the frosting is gone.
Conclusion: Restate the case and invite readers to preheat their ovens.

items.hint: Spine right after the doorway; the pillars march in the thesis's order.
items.explanation: The thesis pre-named its pillars — demand, costs, lasting value — so the body paragraphs must march in exactly that order.
